title: Chapter XXXV

teacherSummary.text: Darcy hands Elizabeth a letter explaining himself: he separated Bingley and Jane believing Jane indifferent and the Bennets improper; and Wickham squandered money, demanded more, and tried to elope with Darcy's 15-year-old sister Georgiana for her fortune.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XXXV,” how does Austen show the letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXXV, how does Austen develop the idea of the letter? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXV develops the idea of the letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of the letter. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXV suggests about the letter. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's point of view and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses point of view in Chapter XXXV to complicate the reader's understanding of the letter. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the letter responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the letter follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXXV and its treatment of the letter. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's point of view and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXXV as evidence for a larger claim about the letter in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the letter. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: an event that might have been arranged although it was really accidental
a main road that charged a toll

satQuestions.passage: Elizabeth awoke the next morning to the same thoughts and meditations which had at length closed her eyes. She could not yet recover from the surprise of what had happened; it was impossible to think of anything else, and totally indisposed for employment, she resolved soon after breakfast to indulge herself in air and exercise. She was proceeding directly to her favourite walk, when the recollection of Mr. Darcy’s sometimes coming there stopped her, and instead of entering the park, she turned up the lane, which led her farther from the turnpike road. The park paling was still the boundary on one side, and she soon passed one of the gates into the ground.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXXV”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does the letter change what we know? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Darcy's letter reveals that an adult man pursued a 15-year-old girl for her money. We will call that what it is.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are obtruded, elopement, turnpike, benefited, decease. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “But last summer he was again most painfully obtruded on my notice.” In this sentence it means: pushed forward unwelcome. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Letters in novels allow characters to speak fully; here the epistolary form reverses the plot. Why does this chapter matter? The letter shifts point of view, forcing Elizabeth (and readers) to re-examine the evidence. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Elizabeth awoke the next morning to the same thoughts and meditations which had at length closed her eyes.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the letter? I circle “turnpike”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find point of view, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for point of view.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Elizabeth awoke the next morning to the same thoughts and meditations which had at length closed her eyes. She could not yet recover from the surprise of what had happened; it was impossible to think of anything else, and totally indisposed for employment, she resolved soon after breakfast to indulge herself in air and exercise. She was proceeding directly to her favourite walk, when the recollection of Mr. Darcy’s sometimes coming there stopped her, and instead of entering the park, she turned up the lane, which led her farther from the turnpike road. The park paling was still the boundary on one side, and she soon passed one of the gates into the ground.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Characterization, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter XXXV develops the idea of the letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the letter, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes the letter. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Wickham, an adult, tried to elope with 15-year-old Georgiana for her fortune. Name this as predatory behavior and grooming, not romance.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Darcy's letter reveals that an adult man pursued a 15-year-old girl for her money. We will call that what it is.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “How does Darcy describe what Wickham did? Why does it matter that Georgiana was fifteen?”
